In environments of structural opacity, the expectation of an ideal situation of complete information leads to a methodological error that feeds case-by-case decisions. Ferraz Jr. delimits this point by stating that decision is not “the establishment of an equitable apportionment among the alternatives”, since that would presuppose the ideal situation of a subject who deliberates “only after having all the relevant data”, being able to enumerate and evaluate the alternatives in advance. The ideal situation is denied by the very existence of the conflict, since the decision corresponds to a “complex procedure” in the face of a situation “characterized by insecurity” <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 305])</2>. In the regime of the IOC, this prevents conditioning protection on an ideal of total transparency or on a model of proof that presupposes full intelligibility of the platform's internal functioning.

The difference between information and practical intelligibility, at the level of legal discourse, reinforces why the formal expansion of clarifications does not resolve the decisive asymmetry of platform consumption. Ferraz Jr. observes that the “absorption of insecurity” does not necessarily mean obtaining consensus and does not have the function of reducing or eliminating incompatibilities. Therefore, in terms of information theory, the absorption of insecurity “should not, then, be confused with the process of eliminating information” <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 1997, p. 44)</2>. The category needs to operate with controllable criteria that allow deciding under insecurity, without turning the absence of complete access to the functioning of the ecosystem into an impediment to attribution.

<1>p. 419</1> The legitimacy of concept formation also depends on a method that preserves the internal coherence of the system and, at the same time, adherence to the object, avoiding both physicalist reductions and dissolving abstractions<2><3>434</3></2>.

Larenz <1>(1997)</1> justifies conceptual construction as a task proper to dogmatics when it needs to operate ordering structures intended to function homogeneously across multiple relations of life. This makes it possible to frame or classify individual legal relations, with attention to the general significance of these institutes for the regulation of human relations, and not to what is historically unique about them <2>Larenz</2><3>(Larenz, 1997, p. 143)</3>. This ordering function is neither neutral nor merely descriptive, since it contributes decisively to jurisprudential stability when problems of valuation are converted into problems of thought and, for that reason, can be treated with greater control through better dogmatic construction of concepts and through the explicitation and understanding of the specificity of the regulation <4>Larenz</4><5>(Larenz, 1997, p. 314)</5>. This key reinforces that the category is not a descriptive ornament, but an instrument for making representable and adjudicable what is at stake in sustained enjoyment, protecting consumer law against formalist blindness and against the abstraction that erases the object under a generic notion of “service”.

The method also makes it possible to reconstruct the legal system as a teleological and open order, still endowed with intrinsic rationality and with directive points of view. In addressing the problem of the system, Larenz maintains that the unity of law is not preserved by a system of general legal concepts, but by an axiological or teleological order structured by general legal principles. From this perspective, the principle, and not the concept, functions as an open standard that requires concretization and only becomes fully graspable in the concretizations it produces <1>Larenz</1><2>(Larenz, 1997, p. 235)</2>. This key makes it possible to integrate new situations without breaking the unity of law, because it shifts the consistency of the legal order to the internal rationality of the directive values and to the continuous work of concretization, instead of depending on a closed catalog of definitions.

In addition, the warning against solutions that promise maximum precision at the cost of emptying is especially pertinent to platform consumption. Citing Kaufmann, Larenz points out that the pursuit of maximum precision of language tends to exact as its price the maximum emptying of content and meaning, as an effect of abstraction taken to the <1>p. 420</1> extreme <2>Larenz</2><3>(Larenz, 1997, p. 190)</3>. In enjoyment ecosystems governed by infrastructure, this risk appears when enjoyment is reduced to residual labels that cannot guide proof, attribution and restoration, precisely in the context in which a criterion capable of capturing the operational density and the relevant variations of the enjoyment bundle is required.

The requirement of controllable criteria for the category is not exhausted in justifying the formation of the concept, since it also sets conditions of institutional verifiability<1><2>435</2></1>. In continuous consumption governed by infrastructure, the risk of elasticity increases precisely where complexity and opacity increase, so that the category is only sustainable if it imposes a verifiable qualification roadmap.

The warning is completed by the critique of theoretical distinctions that, by manipulating elements assessable only at the concrete level, obstruct the application of law and eliminate the applier's burden of argumentation<1><2>436</2></1> <3>Ávila</3><4>(Ávila, 2018, p. 89)</4>. The core of the IOC, therefore, must impose on the interpreter the duty to indicate the elements of the regime used, the connections between those elements and the result, and the reasons why ordinary variations were distinguished from significant degradations

The requirement of controllability is further projected in terms of legal certainty as a methodology for reducing vagueness and institutionally stabilizing decision-making standards. Ávila<1><2>437</2></1> maintains that the focus should shift from “certainty of meaning” to “certainty of criteria”, so as to provide “prior and abstract parameters” that guide the resolution of later and concrete interpretive problems <3>Ávila</3><4>(Ávila, 2011, p. 71)</4>. In the same direction, legal certainty is defined as a requirement of “legal-rational controllability of reconstructive argumentative structures” and as an instrument of protection against “deception, frustration, surprise and arbitrariness” <5>Ávila</5><6>(Ávila, 2011, p. 268)</6>. The result is a rule of <7>p. 421</7> calibration: the category must allow distinguishing, by controllable standards, the ordinary from the relevant and stabilizing expectations without requiring total transparency as a condition of protection.

This requirement also functions as a warning against solutions that promise justice through elasticity, but deliver arbitrariness through lack of standard. In addressing balancing, Ávila requires prior indication of the object and the criteria, stating that, without this, balancing becomes an instrument of arbitrariness, and must be guided by criteria that are “universalizable and legally justifiable” <1>Ávila</1><2>(Ávila, 2011, p. 373)</2>.

In platform consumption, opacity and technical language facilitate both the rhetoric of “it is not possible to know” and the rhetoric of “this is obviously abusive”, and that is why the category needs to block this short circuit by imposing verifiable criteria. These criteria also need to carry an unequivocal negative edge, since the category is not activated by interface preferences, ordinary discomforts of use or mere functional updating, and does not turn the regular exercise of curation or moderation, by itself, into an unlawful act. Calculability, in this context, corresponds to the citizen's capacity to “foresee […] the limits of the intervention of the Public Power” and to know “in advance the scope of discretion” of the State <1>Ávila</1><2>(Ávila, 2011, p. 126)</2>, which requires a standard capable of distinguishing ordinary variations from significant degradations of the enjoyment bundle, preventing both dogmatic abdication and punitive voluntarism.

Under such dogmatic and methodological premises, the core of the IOC can be formulated in a lean and controllable way as an immaterial product whose mode of legal existence is not exhausted in an act of delivery, because it is realized as a position of sustained enjoyment in a technical-organizational environment that maintains, modulates and conditions the acquired utility over time. The object is not confused with isolated “content” nor with an abstract promise of access, but with a bundle of functionalities and significations that makes up the economically offered utility and that remains enjoyable through the continuity of infrastructural conditions of availability, mediation and presentation. Immateriality, in this sense, does not reduce the object to the absence of a medium, but rather identifies that the good offered is graspable by the function and by the regime of enjoyment it establishes, remaining legally qualifiable as a product.

This conceptual core remains compatible with the dogmatic indications already established on the basis of Nunes regarding the functional scope of the concept of product, the durability of continuous services by contractual stipulation and the centrality of supply even when performance depends on complex infrastructure. This set prevents two distinct maneuvers. The first is to expel the immaterial from the field of "product". The second is to use <1>p. 422</1> continuity as a pretext to empty protection and confuse the promised core with a mere technical operation of delivery.

The consolidation of the core of the IOC as an immaterial product, under verifiability locks, does not correspond to the creation of a parallel regime nor to a category external to the CDC. The legal qualification of the fact is not carried out by mechanical subsumption, but by a process of concretion in which norm and factual support refer to each other until the case becomes legally graspable. Reale describes this procedure by stating that the determination of the norm “among the various possible norms” already requires “preliminary reference to the factual element”, and that the applier “not rarely goes from the norm to the fact and vice versa” <1>Reale</1><2>(Reale, 2001, p. 283)</2>. This logic prevents treating the IOC as a label and allows it to be situated as an instrument of decidability within consumer law.

The same requirement of internal integration appears, in Larenz, as a methodological commitment to the coherence of the legal order, instead of classificatory formulas that serve external systematics but fail when the dispute requires delimiting the content and limits of the institute. Criticizing the reduction of legal thought to a general-abstract concept, Larenz observes that an “abbreviated formula” may render services to systematics, but is not “appropriate as a basis for argumentation about the content and the limits” of the institute, since it would obliterate distinctions oriented to social reality and to normative function <1>Larenz</1><2>(Larenz, 1997, p. 318)</2>. In addition, certain definitions have binding meaning and only acquire practical significance “in connection with the legal propositions” in which the term is used, functioning as a normative indication for reading the institute <3>Larenz</3><4>(Larenz, 1997, p. 360)</4>. With this, the qualification of the IOC as an immaterial product presents itself as coherent integration into the CDC, preserving the object as object and avoiding both formalist refusal and dissolution into generic “service”.

Once the anchoring of the IOC in the concept of product of the CDC has been established and its core made explicit in terms compatible with sustained enjoyment, it becomes possible to operate with a category that delimits a legally recognizable object and, therefore, one susceptible to proof, attribution and restoration. The decisive consequence is to remove the conflict from the alternative between a formalism that identifies "delivery" as the one-off provision of access and an undifferentiated language of service that erases what was acquired when utility depends on continuous technical mediations. Continuity ceases to operate as an alibi for lack of protection, because the bond projected in time reinforces the need for criteria that differentiate ordinary variations from relevant degradations of the enjoyment bundle, even if nominal access remains available. Next, the category will be reconstructed in a dual function, as qualification of the object and <1>p. 423</1> as an infrastructure-concept, to reorganize the reading of the offer, of relevant losses and of restoration in continuous consumption under controllable criteria.

The dogmatic anchoring of the IOC finds substrate in the teaching of Luiz Antonio Rizzatto Nunes <1>(2018)</1>, who, in his Curso de Direito do Consumidor, offers a systematic instrumentarium to qualify the elements of the consumer relationship and to deal with border zones between product and service, including in durable and continued supplies. The central utility, in this framing, lies in three points: the definition of product with a deliberately broad scope, including immaterial goods; the operable distinction between product and service as an instrument of qualification; and the compatibility, within the CDC, between protective safeguarding and relationships that extend over time by contractual stipulation and by supply structure. <2>↩</2>

Two works by Miguel Reale offer the key to conversion in dogmatic terms and impose limits against voluntarism and technological moralization. In Lições Preliminares de Direito (2001), what matters is the understanding of law as an experience that is not exhausted in logical form and the description of normative functioning as integration between factual support and evaluative requirement. In Teoria Tridimensional do Direito (1994), what matters is the systematization of specific and concrete tridimensionalism, which rejects the watertight separation between fact, value and norm and describes the normative element as a dialectical integration of the factual-axiological correlation. <1>↩</1>

In this sense, Roberto Mangabeira Unger is drawn upon, in a targeted way, in False Necessity (2004), as a critique of the naturalization of contingent arrangements under the appearance of inevitability. <1>↩</1>

In “False Necessity: Anti-Necessitarian Social Theory in the Service of Radical Democracy”, in our translation, the author (2004) formulates a project of “constructive social theory” structured on two complementary fronts. On one side, he develops an explanatory theory aimed at freeing the understanding of society and history from fatalistic conceptions. On the other, he presents a program of institutional reconstruction oriented toward increasing the revisability of formative contexts. <1>↩</1>

Unger calls “false necessity” the intellectual and political mechanism by which a contingent historical arrangement is taken as if it were the only rational and possible way of organizing social life. The formulation is dry and serves precisely to block the naturalization of the present. Thus, the author describes the genesis of the illusion: “The connection between the themes of false necessity and deepened democracy also runs in the opposite direction. The developed conception of an alternative, promising a way to realize more fully our interests and ideals, puts the will on the side of the imagination. The illusions of false necessity arise because we surrender to the social world, and then begin to mistake present society for possible humanity, giving in to the ideas and attitudes that make the established order seem natural, necessary, or authoritative. By wanting and imagining something else, in a way that lets us see how the something else could arise out of the here and now, we dispel this hallucination. We bring our ideas about society into closer relation with what we repeatedly discover in natural science: that to understand a state of affairs is to grasp its transformative possibilities, seeing the actual in the light of the possible. The central difficulty in our understanding of ourselves and of society is that we cannot mark out the limits of the possible. The possible in society and history is not a well-defined, closed set of transmutations within which actual historical experience has developed as a subset. The possible is just what we can do next, getting there from here. However, so long as we make a living connection between our ideas about how we got here and our ideas about how we can get to the next place, we do not need to stare at what exists and to represent that stare as insight. We can imagine what exists as the resting place and the starting point that it always really is.” <1>Unger</1><2>(Unger, 2004, p. xx)</2>. The reach of the argument is not to deny that material limits exist, but to prevent the language of limit from functioning as a seal of authority. This point is decisive when institutional design presents itself as neutral, as if the concrete way of organizing access, authorization, incentives and sanctions were a technical deduction and not a disputed choice. “Necessity” here becomes a rhetoric of disclaiming responsibility. By describing the present as only one possible humanity among others, Unger shifts the center of the debate. What seemed inevitable becomes debatable again, and what seemed technical becomes attributable again in terms of decision and consequences. <3>↩</3>

Unger's refusal of fatalism is not moral, it is a methodological position within social theory. At the core of his work, the author describes his project as “relentlessly anti-necessitarian” and states that it “carries to extremes the thesis that everything in society is politics, mere politics” <1>Unger</1><2>(Unger, 2004, p. 1)</2>. The sense is operational, given that, if the social order is made, it can be unmade and remade, and this preserves both the possibility of strong explanation and the possibility of institutional reconstruction. In his introduction, Mangabeira Unger insists on the same key by saying that one can “carry to the hilt the idea that the organization of society is made” and, even so, “rebel against the worlds we have built”, even recognizing that these rebellions may be interrupted and resumed <3>Unger</3><4>(Unger, 2004, p. xvii)</4>. The historical point of the work comes by the genealogical route. Unger maintains that consolidated institutions are not “the natural and necessary realization of practical imperatives and ideological commitments”; they are better understood as “strange and surprising” products of a history of conflict, “a second nature, a provisional fate” <5>Unger</5><6>(Unger, 2004, p. xxxvi)</6>. Thus, genealogy fulfills the precise function of attacking the reflex of treating the prevailing arrangement as destiny. When contingency is restored at the origin, the field of the revisable in the present is reopened. <7>↩</7>

One of the typical operations of immunizing institutional design consists in shifting power relations to the register of a supposed neutral necessity of coordination. Unger gives the reader a very explicit map of how modern legal thought usually tries to “tame the dangers of power” by sectors, as if each domain had its own antidote. In this grammar, the organization of work appears associated with “voluntary agreement and impersonal technical necessity” <1>Unger</1><2>(Unger, 2004, p. 301-302)</2>. This formula, read sympathetically, assumes a civilizing promise of combining autonomy and efficiency. Read critically, it shows how the appeal to technique can function as a shortcut to close the discussion about design, hierarchy and control. The critique becomes even more concrete when Unger describes the combination of “widespread supervisory discretion” and “the facade of a regime of contract”, which would be justified as “a requirement of impersonal technical necessity”. The error, for him, lies in crediting this claim with the status of ultimate truth, as if it “transcended the actual sequence of conflicts and truces that had produced these results” <3>Unger</3><4>(Unger, 2004, p. 513)</4>. Thus, the less grounded the invocation of necessity and the more the underlying reality involves subjugation, the more glaring the contrast between the ideal picture of the system of contracts and property and the everyday reality of work. The usefulness of such a construction, here, lies not in denying coordination, but in exposing the ideological function of the label “impersonal” when it serves to conceal institutional choice and block accountability. <5>↩</5>

Mangabeira Unger describes the naturalization of the arrangement not as a mere theoretical error, but as a cumulative political effect. He points to the effort to “depoliticize the basic structure of rights and economic policy” and observes that, once the original conflicts and uncertainties are forgotten, the institutional settlement assumes a “specious semblance of naturalness and necessity”, although it is no more necessary than “the interests and the illusions, the tactical achievements and the tactical failures” that consolidated it <1>Unger</1><2>(Unger, 2004, p. 178)</2>. The statement is strong because it puts the institution back in the place of a tactical and historical result, not of an inevitable functional requirement. In the introduction, the author names the error, distinguishing “institutional fetishism” and “structure fetishism”. The first is failing to understand that conceptions such as “representative democracy” or “market economy” have no single, natural or necessary expression in a determinate set of rules and practices. The second is failing to recognize that one can change not only the content, but the quality of the institutional and ideological order, including its relation to the power by which it is contested, and for that reason it comes to be lived as an entrenched natural fact <3>Unger</3><4>(Unger, 2004, p. cxxii)</4>. The psychological mechanism of closure appears when the author maintains: “There is entrapment in a divisive and specialized order of society and culture. That is the form of entrapment that the radicalization of democratic experimentalism most directly undermines. The concepts of institutional and structure fetishism describe two of its more important manifestations in our ideas. They show how we become accomplices to our own enslavement. We are also entrapped, more generally, by the naturalization of the social world through repetition. Repetition in society and culture is a kind of incantation, leading us, through our inability to produce or endure permanent novelty and to be ever new, to accept a habitual form of life as a second nature. We spring the trap by changing the relation between repetition and disruption. We must so reform our arrangements and practices — including our practices of discourse in technical disciplines like legal analysis or political economy — that the very activities by which we reproduce our second nature create opportunities and provide tools for its fragmentary, but motivated and cumulative remaking.” <5>Unger</5><6>(Unger, 2004, p. cxxiii)</6>. Thus, what seems mere routine becomes an effective “institutional spell”. <7>↩</7>

In this framing, two works by Tércio Sampaio Ferraz Jr. are drawn upon. The first is <1>Introdução ao Estudo do Direito: </1> <2>Técnica, Decisão, Dominação</2> (2003), for its approach to law as a decision-making phenomenon and to dogmatics as a technology aimed at the decidability of conflicts. The second is <3>Direito, Retórica e Comunicação: subsídios </3> <4>para uma pragmática do discurso jurídico</4> (1997), for the pragmatic cut of legal discourse and for the way in which decision absorbs insecurity without confusing this operation with a mere accumulation of information. The approach to dogmatics as technology provides operational justification for the construction of the IOC as a category capable of guiding proof and decision. <5>↩</5>

It is in this framing that Karl Larenz is drawn upon, in <1>Metodologia da Ciência do Direito</1> (1997), as technical vocabulary to maintain that, in the face of new forms of supply and of continued enjoyment, the adequate response is not to abandon the system nor to invent an “other law”, but to qualify the phenomenon by criteria internal to the legal order, preserving teleological coherence and decision-making capacity. <2>↩</2>

At this point, Humberto Ávila is drawn upon, in <1>Teoria dos Princípios</1> (2018), as a discipline of precision intended to prevent categories and standards from becoming a performative language of decision. Conceptual clarity has an institutional function by expanding means of control and preventing argumentation from descending into “capricious decisionism” <2>Ávila</2><3>(Ávila, 2018, p. 45)</3>. <4>↩</4>

Ávila formulates this critique in the context of the attempt to distinguish rules and principles at the abstract level. The problem, for him, is the confusion between a preliminary moment of signification (prima facie) and the conclusive moment of application (all things considered), which leads doctrine to transport into general theory elements that can only be assessed in the concrete case and, with that, to turn categories into alibis. The distinction between normative species should “relieve, by structuring it, the burden of argumentation of the applier of the law”, “reduce - eliminate, never - the need for [the duty] to be justified” <1>Ávila</1><2>(Ávila, 2018, p. 88)</2>. When, however, the classification comes to “manipulate, for the abstract interpretation of norms, elements that can only be assessed at the concrete level of application”, it “ends up obstructing it” and, “instead of relieving the burden of argumentation of the applier of the law, eliminates it” <3>Ávila</3><4>(Ávila, 2018, p. 89)</4>. <5>↩</5>

For this framing, <1>Segurança Jurídica: Entre Permanência, Mudança e Realização no Direito </1> <2>Tributário</2> <3>Ávila</3><4>(Ávila, 2011)</4> is drawn upon, whose conceptual architecture reconstructs legal certainty as a norm-principle structured by cognoscibility, reliability and calculability. The decisive point is to shift the discussion from the promise of a fixed meaning to the requirement of prior and controllable criteria. <5>↩</5>

The anchoring of the immaterial object of consumption in the concept of product of Article 3, paragraph 1, of the CDC ensures the dogmatic insertion of the phenomenon and preserves the intelligibility of what is acquired in platform-governed enjoyment, without reducing the relationship to a one-off event of delivery nor dissolving it into an undifferentiated notion of service. Even so, the qualification as an immaterial product does not settle the central problem of the regime of the IOC. In continuous consumption, utility is not realized as isolated “content”, but as a position of sustained enjoyment in a technical-organizational environment that maintains, modulates and conditions, over time, the enjoyment bundle through internal rules, curation, reconfiguration and <1>enforcement</1> executed by design. The next step consists in reconstructing the IOC as an infrastructure-concept, capable of operating simultaneously as a form of qualification of the object and as an interpretive key to the supply regime, reorganizing the reading of the offer, the identification of relevant losses and the orientation of restoration when degradation manifests itself as erosion of the enjoyment bundle, even without total interruption of formal access.

The methodological justification for this operation finds in Karl Larenz <1>(1997)</1> an especially adequate vocabulary. Conceptual construction is not presented as a classificatory ornament, but as an instrument for making recurring conflicts decidable in a stable and verifiable way, without requiring the solution to depend on moral impressions, on episodic readings of clauses, or on mechanical subsumptions insensitive to the contemporary form of supply. The question is explicit when it is stated that dogmatics “makes ‘a decisive contribution to jurisprudential stability, when its problems of valuation are resolved into problems of thought and, as such, can be better mastered, in the language familiar to it, through a better dogmatic construction of the concept, through uncovering, understanding and mastering the specificity of the regulation’” <2>Larenz</2><3>(Larenz, 1997, p. 313-314)</3>.

In the regime of the IOC, this “specificity of the regulation” corresponds to the fact that the acquired utility is administered over time by infrastructural conditions of availability, visibility, circulation, permanence and sanction, so that the controversy is not clarified by a snapshot of delivery nor by a generic label of performance.

<1>p. 424</1> This reconstruction demands, however, an additional caution. The conceptual effort must remain internal to the CDC and to its protective teleology, without inaugurating an autonomous merely “digital” vocabulary and without opening space for an elasticity that replaces criterion with rhetoric. The dogmatic risk of dissolving abstraction, already warned of by Larenz, appears when a category serves external systematics but fails precisely where density is required to discuss content and limits. In platform consumption, this erasure produces a direct effect. The object disappears from the analysis, the offer loses its delimiting function and restoration becomes erratic when degradation occurs as persistent erosion of the enjoyment bundle, without absolute blocking of formal access.

The symmetrical critique is equally relevant. The pursuit of precision can buy apparent certainty at the price of emptying the concept, producing a category that is formally clean and materially blind — a risk already pointed out by Larenz regarding abstraction taken to the extreme. For the IOC, this means that insistence on rigid oppositions or on undifferentiated labels delivers a language incapable of seeing relevant losses in the concrete case and incapable of sustaining proof, attribution and restoration in continuous consumption. The reconstruction of the IOC as an infrastructure-concept aims to block these two falls without abandoning the unity of the system, preserving the intelligibility of the object and, at the same time, incorporating infrastructure as a constitutive dimension of the mode of existence of enjoyment.

The systematic coherence of this operation presupposes understanding the legal system as a teleological order able to integrate new situations by internal criteria, oriented by function and by meaning — a characteristic already formulated by Larenz as a structural trait of the internal system. The consequence is that the relevant question is not limited to verifying whether there was initial enabling of access, but brings supply back to the promise that is realized over time and to the infrastructural conditions that make it enjoyable, because it is on this plane that the content of what was acquired and the scope of its protection under the CDC are decided.

The requirement of conceptual reconstruction also depends on an institutional justification aimed at decidability under uncertainty. In platform-governed consumption, protection cannot be held hostage to an ideal of full intelligibility of the ecosystem, nor can it require total transparency as a condition for recognizing relevant non-performance. From the already established perspective that legal decision operates as a complex procedure in the face of insecurity, and not as a rational choice in a scenario of complete information, the reconstruction of the IOC as an infrastructure-concept assumes the function of a dogmatic technology of decidability, by providing a grammar to recognize relevant losses and guide attribution and restoration even when the execution of supply remains partially opaque.

<1>p. 425</1> This same requirement appears at the level of legal communication. In environments marked by structural asymmetry of intelligibility, shifting the axis to the promise of control through accumulation of information tends to produce the opposite effect, turning protection into a hostage of an idealized situation of deliberation. Ferraz Jr. criticizes this approach by maintaining that linking decision and consensus immediately turns the “rational” decision into an idealized model. In this model, all the relevant data would be available from the outset and all the alternatives could be enumerated and evaluated in advance, which is incompatible both with non-controllable variables and with the very structure of the conflict <2>Jr.</2><3>(Ferraz Jr., 1997, p. 43)</3>. In the regime of the IOC, dogmatics must operate with previously structured criteria for qualifying the object and reading the enjoyment bundle, on pain of turning opacity into an alibi of indeterminability or of reducing the debate to generic labels such as “service”.

The counterfactual stabilization of normative expectations, already established earlier in a methodological key, operates, in platform consumption, as a block on two recurring maneuvers. The first reduces delivery to the formal provision of access and treats the nominal persistence of content as eliminating the possibility of relevant non-performance. The second dissolves the object into a vague and reconfigurable performance, converting restoration into an oscillation between shallow restitutions and case-by-case assessments. When the promise is recognized as a normative reference, the category can maintain the value core of what was acquired as an anchor for identifying relevant losses, even when enjoyment is modulated over time by curation, visibility, ranking, internal rules and sanctions executed by design.

At this point, the regime of the IOC requires recognizing that enjoyment does not occur “despite” the ecosystem, but through a layer of governance that operates as practical normativity. Here, the contribution of Eros Roberto Grau makes it possible to describe this layer with legal precision and without dissolving the argument into a general sociology of private power, because it shifts the criterion of the legal from the state monopoly to the presence of functional coercion exercised by a social organization over a delimited group.

On platforms, this coercion is not exhausted in the clause. It is realized in the combination of internal rules, interface architecture and <1>enforcement</1> mechanisms that condition access, permanence, visibility and utility of what was acquired, converting the functioning of the environment into a regime of conduct. What matters, for the analysis of the IOC, is that this normativity is part of the very mode of execution of the promise, because it defines what counts as possible, stable and recognized enjoyment within the ecosystem.

<1>p. 426</1> Recognizing practical normativity, however, is not equivalent to declaring every technical decision unlawful, nor to turning ordinary interface frictions into abuse. The objective is to prevent technique from functioning as automatic shielding against attribution when the design and execution of the ecosystem significantly reconfigure the promised enjoyment bundle, shifting risk to the consumer under the appearance of a simple “update” or “operational adjustment”.

On such bases, the functional qualification of the IOC can be formulated in an operable way. Infrastructure does not appear as a mere technical context accompanying a previously delivered object. It is part of the form of fulfillment of the promise of enjoyment, because it is through it that conditions of availability, presentation, circulation, permanence and sanction that make the acquired utility effectively enjoyable are maintained and modulated over time. Reconstructing the IOC as an infrastructure-concept means qualifying the object according to its legal-economic mode of existence in continuous consumption, preserving the intelligibility of what was acquired without reducing supply to a snapshot of delivery nor dissolving it into an undifferentiated generic performance.

From this operator, the object can be described as a bundle of functionalities and significations administered throughout the relationship, coupled with permissions and limits of use, regimes of visibility and ordering, metrics and signals of recognition, and mechanisms of curation and <1>enforcement</1> executed by design. Enjoyment ceases to be a simple initial enabling and becomes a sustained position in the ecosystem, whose utility depends on the continuity of infrastructural conditions that organize expectations and distribute consequences. The category does not indefinitely expand the unlawful act nor moralize technical choices. It stabilizes a grammar to identify the core of the promised enjoyment bundle and to distinguish, by controllable criteria, between ordinary modulations of the regime and legally relevant significant degradations, including when nominal access persists.

Closing the item also requires making explicit, clearly, the negative edge of the reconstruction. The reconfigurability of the environment does not turn every update, interface adjustment, change in ranking or ordinary curation choice into unlawfulness. What becomes legally relevant is significant, persistent degradation recognizable by criteria, that which alters the core of economically offered utility or structurally lowers the conditions of enjoyment that gave meaning to the acquisition. With this, the discussion ceases to oscillate between formalism and abstraction and comes to require parameters of recognition, evidence and limits of application, so that the legal response remains proportional, verifiable and stable. Once this functional qualification is established, it is possible to advance to the criteria of <1>p. 427</1> incidence, proof and restoration of the regime of the IOC, now with a conceptual operator capable of keeping the object as object and, at the same time, incorporating infrastructural governance as a legally relevant dimension of supply.

Controllability presupposes an elementary discipline of method, which requires identifying which examination is being applied and separating planes that cannot be treated as synonyms. Ávila warns that confusing distinct concrete examinations makes the correct application of law unfeasible, because each one mobilizes its own relations and parameters and may lead to different results <1>Ávila</1><2>(Ávila, 2018, p. 223)</2>. In the regime of the IOC, this warning prevents heterogeneous discussions from being compressed into generic labels such as “service failure”, “policy change” or “moderation”, without clarification of what is being tested and what needs to be demonstrated. The category only remains operable when it forces the separation of the qualification of the object, the identification of the promised enjoyment bundle, the recognition of relevant degradation, the attribution of responsibility and the criteria of restoration, preventing these planes from being confused and generating unstable conclusions.

The institutional usefulness of this separation lies in exposing the structure of reasoning and allowing rational control of the way in which other norms are applied. Ávila observes that, in the application of law, a reasoning aimed at the incidence of other norms of the legal order is always carried out, and that these examinations investigate the way in which such norms should be applied<1><2>438</2></1> <3>Ávila</3><4>(Ávila, 2018, p. 225)</4>. With this, the role of methodological categories as instruments of verifiability is established. In terms of the IOC, each criterion must correspond to an identifiable test, with recognizable parameters and controllable results, so as to allow assessing whether the decision followed a justifiable path or merely covered a discretionary choice with technical vocabulary.

<1>p. 428</1> The IOC only fulfills a dogmatic function when it operates as a filter and as a roadmap. As a filter, it defines what enters and what remains outside the field of incidence, preventing any digital relationship with an appearance of continuity from being absorbed by the category and also preventing the supplier from expelling the conflict from the CDC through strategic labeling. As a roadmap, it forces qualification to follow a controllable sequence, making explicit what needs to be demonstrated for the language of the IOC to make sense and for the discussion not to dissolve into vague impressions about “experience”, “community” or “moderation”.

The first field covered by the criteria is the promised object, understood as an enjoyment bundle. The relevant question is not whether some “content” was available at some point, but what utility was economically offered in terms of functionalities and significations that, in the regime of the IOC, constitute what was acquired. This requires identifying the core of the bundle from the relevant promise and from the elements that, in the concrete arrangement, make that utility exist as an enjoyable thing. The criterion is not satisfied with ornamental lists of functionalities nor with generic advertising slogans. It requires identifying which central functions organize the legitimate expectation of enjoyment and, consequently, delimiting which alterations may reach the core of the object even when the formal continuity of access is preserved.

The second field is the position of sustained enjoyment. In continuous consumption, the acquisition inaugurates a position in the ecosystem and not a delivery exhausted in an instant. This position is the mode of existence of the object over time, since the effective possibility of use, circulation and permanence in the promised form depends on it. Recognizing it means treating as legally relevant the elements that define the consumer's permanence in the regime of enjoyment, without converting mere ordinary discomforts into legal losses. The incidence of the legal regime of the IOC presupposes that utility is enjoyed as a continued bond and that the execution of supply is inseparable from the maintenance of that position.

The third field is infrastructural governance as the mode of execution of supply. The IOC does not merely describe an environment around the object. Infrastructure is incorporated as a constitutive dimension of delivery, because it is through it that internal rules, curation, modulations of visibility, parameters of participation and sanction mechanisms are implemented. Qualification requires demonstrating that enjoyment depends on a technical-organizational arrangement that continuously administers conditions relevant to the promised utility. The filter here is decisive, since the presence of technical mediation in a trivial sense is not enough. What matters is the existence of internal criteria and executive mechanisms that structurally shape the experience of enjoyment and distribute consequences to the consumer.

<1>p. 429</1> The fourth field is the typical possibility of relevant degradation without total rupture. The IOC is only justified if it can see losses that manifest themselves as persistent erosion of the enjoyment bundle, even if nominal access is preserved. The qualification roadmap must require the demonstration of a pattern of degradation that is not confused with ordinary variations, one-off instabilities or neutral interface adjustments. It is a matter of delimiting the zone in which enjoyment continues to exist formally, but is lowered, emptied or reconfigured so as to frustrate the core of offered utility or to reorder the consumer's position in the ecosystem in terms incompatible with the promise that justified the acquisition.

With these fields, the IOC ceases to be an explanatory label and comes to function as an instrument of screening and of disciplining the debate. Incidence is not decided by technological intuition nor by automatic deference to the contract, but by the cumulative presence of verifiable elements of the regime, which allows stabilizing a path of qualification.

The construction of incidence criteria is neither a classificatory luxury nor an attempt to invent new law for the digital. It responds to the need to make recurring conflicts decidable in a stable way, without depending on variable intuitions about technology and without resorting to generic labels that erase the object. The filter of the IOC cannot ignore the structural traits of platform-governed consumption nor, at the opposite extreme, aim to capture each and every discomfort of digital use. Incidence criteria cannot depend on full access to the algorithm, <1>logs</1> and internal rules as a condition of possibility, since that would turn the IOC into an impracticable category, reserved for exceptional cases.

Practicability, however, requires dogmatic rigor, and not relaxation. Under two simultaneous pressures, the binding to norms and the need to decide, legal discourse demands specialized technique and the production of doubts oriented to action <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 47])</2>. Under this horizon, already established earlier as a functional cut aimed at the decidability of conflicts, the institutional gain is to stabilize expectations counterfactually, since norms express expectations whose duration is maintained regardless of the fulfillment or non-fulfillment of the empirically expected action <3>Jr.</3><4>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 104])</4>. For the IOC, the criteria must operate with possible proof and controllable inferences, capable of stabilizing expectations about the core of the enjoyment bundle even when the ecosystem tries to naturalize opacity and reconfigurability as if they were indisputable facts.

This requirement of possible proof separates the inaccessible as a technical detail from the demonstrable as a structured effect of supply. What matters for incidence is not proving “how” the algorithm decides at a microscopic level, but demonstrating that there is infrastructural governance relevant to the acquired utility and that it operates with stability <1>p. 430</1> sufficient to produce patterns of enjoyment and of relevant degradation without total rupture of access. With this, opacity ceases to function as a condition of unenforceability.

Recognizing infrastructural governance as a constitutive element of the IOC requires admitting that, in certain ecosystems, an effective system of rules and sanctions operates that bears on a delimited group and organizes the very possibility of enjoyment. Along the lines of Grau <1>(2008)</1>, this institutional datum can be described as practical normativity, that is, a way of guiding conduct and imposing conformity that produces concrete effects without depending on state status. This reading does not attribute to the platform the condition of a State nor presume unlawfulness. It serves, rather, to qualify effective normativity as a component of supply and, therefore, as a relevant element for assessing the mode of execution of the promise to the consumer, especially when rules, architecture and <2>enforcement</2> mechanisms come to define, in practice, the continuity, integrity and meaning of what was acquired.

The same idea is expressed when it is stated that the State is not the only social organization capable of positing law, that is, of producing posited law, and that it is necessary to break with the conception according to which law is necessarily a creature of the State <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2008, p. 78)</2>. In platform-governed consumption, utility is not realized despite internal rules, curation, modulations of circulation and sanction, but through these mechanisms. This allows treating governance as a component of the legally relevant fact, without converting every form of governance into abuse.

This normativity should also not be naturalized as “spontaneous order”. Grau makes explicit that the expression “legal order of the market” indicates that the market posits its legal order, not the order that it is, but the order that it establishes <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2008, p. 324)</2>. With this, governance ceases to be presented as a technical fatality and comes to be treated as an instituted arrangement. Moreover, the reading avoids an unproductive sociologization by recognizing that law is not a simple external representation of social reality, but a functional level of the social whole and a constitutive element of the mode of social production <3>Grau</3><4>(Grau, 2008, p. 19-20)</4>. In the regime of the IOC, this authorizes reading material and organizational layers as constitutive of the acquired utility, without shifting the argument to a broad sociological diagnosis and without presuming unlawfulness.

The mere existence of moderation, <1>rankings</1>, community rules or interface adjustments is not enough to trigger the operator of the IOC. Ordinary updates, regular curation, anti-abuse interventions and changes that do not reach the functional core of the enjoyment bundle remain in the normal field of execution and do not constitute relevant degradation by definition. What matters is the structural dependence of utility on a continuous executive <2>p. 431</2> governance, in intensity and centrality sufficient for nominal access not to exhaust delivery and for the experience to be degradable without total rupture.

The cut is also not sustainable if “signification” enters as interpretive cosmetics. On platforms, part of the value offered may be anchored in regimes of meaning that organize conduct, expectation and recognition. Umberto Eco<1><2>439</2></1> (1997) provides the technical key for treating sign and code as operative dimensions of experience. By indicating that connotation, because it is shared, is “translated into a system of expectations” and “will be foreseen by a connotative lexicon”<3><4>440</4></3><5>Eco</5><6>(Eco, 1997, p. 29)</6>, it is established that the sign coordinates practical predictions. This matters when the promised utility depends on visibility, reputation, <7>status</7>, <8>ranking</8>, belonging and forms of recognition administered by the ecosystem. In these cases, signification is part of the enjoyment bundle as a condition of use.

This point gains density when the code is understood as a structure of acceptability and intelligibility. Eco maintains that the acceptability of an expression depends on the code and that it would be an exaggerated reduction to state that the code fixes only content <1>Eco</1><2>(Eco, 2000, p. 145)</2>. In platform-governed enjoyment, this key describes how grammars of interaction and regimes of classification modulate valid participation, legitimate visibility and admissible circulation. Thus, the code structure operates as a condition of intelligibility of use and, in certain regimes, as a controllable dimension of the object.

The third piece is the reading of signs as forces with social effects. Eco observes that a theory of codes is mainly interested in signs as social forces <1>Eco</1><2>(Eco, 2000, p. 109)</2>, which makes it possible to recognize relevant losses that manifest themselves as a persistent lowering of recognition, reach or belonging when these elements were offered as part of the value. At the limit, Eco maintains that subjects are shaped by the <3>p. 432</3> possibilities that the form of the world produced by signs allows them to occupy <4>Eco</4><5>(Eco, 1991, p. 62)</5>. The argument reinforces that the environment administers subject positions and conditions of participation, which can be sold as utility and, when they are, can be part of the enjoyment bundle.

The consequence is to circumscribe when the semiotic dimension enters and when it should stay out. It is part of the bundle when it makes up the core of utility economically offered and enjoyed as a position in the ecosystem, that is, when the platform sells, explicitly or functionally, effects of recognition, visibility, circulation, reputation, belonging or status as part of the value of what was acquired. The dimension is not part of it when it is a matter of aesthetics, <1>marketing</1>, generic advertising narrative or diffuse satisfaction without an identifiable functional core and without a structural link to the position of sustained enjoyment. The intention is to avoid two abuses: seeing semiotics in everything and dissolving the filter; or always treating it as peripheral and blinding the concept to regimes in which the object is a socially operative position sustained by rules of visibility and sanction.

Such a filter requires, then, a connection with the dogmatic basis of consumption, without requiring, for that, the inauguration of a new microsystem. Cláudia Lima Marques describes the contemporary shift toward massified, adhesion-based and long-term contractual forms, marked by symbiosis between products and services and by technological intermediation on consumer platforms <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2024, [p. 2])</2>. Her doctrine makes it possible to recognize that the form of performance depends on continuous technical mediations, which reinforces the need for incidence criteria capable of separating ordinary variations from relevant degradations of the bundle. The author also highlights that vulnerabilities and harms may arise from the <3>design</3> and the conduct of the intermediary, who operates as a <4>gatekeeper</4> and influences the time, manner and outcome of the bond, including through data manipulation <5>Marques</5><6>(Marques, 2024, [p. 3])</6>. This fit reinforces the thesis of structural vulnerability and the need for criteria that do not depend on total transparency of the black box.

The consumerist anchoring also resolves the risk of absolutizing <1>design</1>. When it is recognized that it is possible to sanction cases of deceptive design and the provisions of Article 39 of the CDC<2><3>441</3></2> are linked to dark patterns, <4>design</4> is put back in its correct place, as an economically oriented and legally qualifiable commercial practice, and not as aesthetic neutrality <5>Bergstein</5><6>(Marques; Mendes; Bergstein, 2023, [p. 4])</6>. In the same sense, the statement that, in the digital society, vulnerability may assume an architectural character, and that such <7>p. 433</7> vulnerabilities are a product of the digital consumer markets themselves, reinforces that the architecture of the environment is part of the economic mechanism of supply <8>Mucelin</8><9>(Marques; Mucelin, 2022, p. 18)</9>. This does not presume abuse, but justifies the need for an operator that identifies when architecture appears as a constitutive condition of the acquired utility.

Here, Rizzatto Nunes offers dogmatic support for essential locks of the filter. Technical vulnerability appears as structural asymmetry, since the consumer is the weak link of the relationship, especially because they do not have access to the information that makes up the productive process, so that their choice is already born reduced <1>Nunes</1><2>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 122])</2>. Presentation and visual impact also enter as legally relevant conduct, insofar as suppliers may resort to visual impact and catchphrases to conceal relevant aspects of the offer <3>Nunes</3><4>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 370])</4>. Moreover, in interpreting Article 30<5><6>442</6></5>, the author recognizes that the offer may arise from the mere presentation of the product in the shop window <7>Nunes</7><8>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 312])</8>, which supports reading the digital shop window as a binding offer. With this, the IOC remains within the CDC, without demonizing the interface and without allowing the interface to be treated as irrelevant.

Thus, therefore, the incidence criteria of the IOC can be formulated as a qualification roadmap in a controllable sequence. The first element is economic-functional. An identifiable core of utility is required, promised and enjoyed as acquired, reconstructible from the relevant offer and from the effective mode of enjoyment. The second element is structural. Utility is realized as a position of enjoyment sustained over time, and not as an exhausted event. The third element is infrastructural. Utility depends on governed conditions, such as access, permanence, visibility, circulation and sanction, administered by continuous execution. The fourth element is one of legal relevance. There is a typical possibility of relevant degradation of the bundle without total rupture of access, in a persistent and substantive way, and not as a one-off discomfort.

With the incidence criteria outlined, the limits of exclusion fulfill an equally institutional function. They prevent the IOC from becoming a language “of atmosphere” for digital disputes and ensure that the concept operates as an instrument of demarcation with precision and legitimacy.

The first limit is one-off access without a position of sustained enjoyment. When performance is episodic and exhausted in the act, there is no reason to mobilize an operator built <1>p. 434</1> to describe continuity and administration of permanence, since the classic dogmatics of service is sufficient to resolve the dispute.

The second limit is the hypothesis in which the platform functions as a channel or shop window, but does not govern, in structural terms, the acquired utility, lacking the infrastructural centrality characteristic of the IOC. This is the case that excludes, in principle, the <1>marketplace</1> that provides positioning and customer acquisition services by advertising means, but does not exercise relevant material interference over the effective governance of subsequent commercial operations. This limit, however, cannot be read as a clause removing <2>marketplace</2> platforms from the regime of the IOC. Once the applicability of Article 29 of the CDC<3><4>443</4></3> to qualify legal entities in a factual position of vulnerability is admitted, the regime proves fully pertinent when the immaterial object in question is the enjoyment bundle in a sustained position exploited as a product in the B2B<5><6>444</6></5> market by the holder and offered, through the <7>marketplace</7> platform, to the <8>seller </8>(vendedor).

The third limit falls on situations in which the symbolic or semiotic value is functionally accessory and is not part of the core of the promised enjoyment bundle. In these hypotheses, signification is not reconstructible from traits of supply and of infrastructural execution, degrading into an indeterminate expectation about social reaction. The function of this limit is to block the unmotivated use of the regime of the IOC to contest alterations incapable of depredating the core of the value offered. Therefore, as a rule, predominantly aesthetic alterations fall outside the reach of the concept, except when, in the concrete case, they make up a convergent set of signals able to sustain objective recognition of an unlawful act of architecture through structural indications of abusive teleology.

The fourth limit covers ordinary variations of the ecosystem that do not constitute relevant and persistent degradation of the bundle, such as updates, interface adjustments, anti-abuse measures, regular moderation and one-off instabilities. It is a protocol limit that, in general terms, introduces a reasonableness clause. At the same time, the <1>design</1> of the concept must allow recognizing when the ordinary exacerbates its own function and comes to collaborate with macrostructures responsible for practices of structural exploitation of the semiotic vulnerability of consumer users.

<1>p. 435</1> The fifth limit is the case in which the core of the conflict is something else, such as a classic one-off quality defect, undue charging, localized misleading advertising or specific non-performance of an offer. In these hypotheses, common consumer dogmatics tends to resolve the dispute without real gain in mobilizing the IOC.

The negative edge is not an aesthetic caution, but a condition of operability of the concept. Larenz <1>(1997, p. 311)</1> recalls that open standards are not purely and simply devoid of content and are not confused with empty pseudo-normative formulas compatible with any concrete form of behavior.

The requirement of limit is also dogmatic. Ferraz Jr. <1>(2003, [p. 172])</1> observes that dogmatics grasps the legal order systematically to meet the requirements of the decidability of conflicts and that this set needs to present reasonably precise contours. From this perspective, system implies a notion of limit, that is, an abstract line that makes it possible to identify what is inside, what enters, what leaves and what remains outside <2>Jr.</2><3>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 172])</3>. The negative edge preserves the system from collapse by overreach and prevents the IOC from invading conflicts whose core is already resolvable by traditional keys of the CDC.

In these terms, the IOC ceases to be an elegant description of platforms and comes to operate as a technology of qualification. The category imposes a controllable sequence of questions about promise, position of enjoyment, infrastructural mode of execution and relevant degradation, with demonstrable and contestable parameters, keeping the conflict within the CDC without inaugurating a microsystem and without accepting strategic escape through labeling of supply. At the same time, the limits of exclusion prevent ordinary variations and regular curation from being treated as degradation by definition. The IOC comes to function as a language of proof and of screening, and not as a vocabulary of atmosphere.

With this design structured, it becomes possible to advance to relevant losses and criteria of attribution without contaminating the discussion with doubts about what was acquired and what the legal mode of existence of that utility is over time. Criteria and exclusions thus fulfill the institutional function of turning the IOC into an applicable operator, with roadmap and limits, capable of guiding the reconstruction of supply and preparing the analysis of what counts as legally relevant degradation and what remains as an ordinary variation of the regime.

Ávila makes clear that reasonableness, proportionality and the prohibition of excess do not enter the game as an additional “meaning” of norms. They operate at a second level, rationally organizing how other norms should be applied, hence the choice of the term “postulate”. “This shows that these examinations investigate the way in which other norms should be applied, whether by establishing the criteria, or by establishing the measures. In any case, the requirements arising from reasonableness, proportionality and the prohibition of excess bear upon other norms not, however, to attribute meaning to them, but to rationally structure their application. There is always another norm behind the application of reasonableness, proportionality and excessiveness. For this reason, it is appropriate to treat them as metanorms. And, since they structure the application of other norms, without being confused with them, it is appropriate to refer to them with another nomenclature. Hence the use of the term ‘postulate’, to indicate a norm that structures the application of others.” <1>Ávila</1><2>(Ávila, 2018, p. 225)</2>. <3>↩</3>
