The passage from one-off consumption to platform-sustained enjoyment exposes a structural tension in the vocabulary of the CDC. Supply is no longer described as a simple <1>p. 436</1> event of delivery, nor as an episodic performance exhausted in initial execution. When the acquired utility depends on a technical-organizational environment in continuous operation, the object remains identifiable as an enjoyment bundle, but its legal existence is realized over time through acts of maintenance, modulation, curation and execution of rules.

In this context, the product-service dichotomy tends to become a true semantic trap, given that at times it paralyzes the analysis as if the classification settled the regime, and at other times it dissolves the object into a generic “service” and renders invisible relevant losses that do not manifest themselves as total interruption. The task, therefore, is to put the dichotomy back in its functional place, preserving the intelligibility of what was acquired as an immaterial product and recognizing, at the same time, that continued enjoyment requires a reading of supply capable of capturing duties and conduct that are projected over time.

With this, the axis of the problem ceases to be the abstract framing of the object and becomes the interpretive operationalization of supply in a durable regime of enjoyment. What matters is a mode of reading that allows capturing duties, conduct and relevant losses when utility is not realized as an inaugural instant, but as permanent execution administered by a platform. The product-service dichotomy, here, is only useful if it functions as a tool for calibrating effects, without reducing what was acquired to instantaneous delivery and without dissolving it into undifferentiated performance.

At this point, consumer doctrine offers well-known instruments for dealing with long-term relationships, successive execution and duties projected over time. Claudia Lima Marques<1><2>445</2></1>, in multiple reference works, reconstructs the incidence of the CDC on contract theory, emphasizing objective good faith, protection of trust, socialization of the contract and the centrality of adhesion bonds, so as to maintain that protection is not exhausted in formation and is projected onto execution.

Platform-governed continued enjoyment brings supply closer to consumer relations that are not explained by instantaneous purchase and sale, since they are structured as complex long-term bonds and tend to install the consumer in a position of practical dependence vis-à-vis the supplier and its chain. Claudia Lima Marques describes this <1>p. 437</1> structure when dealing with “new contracts or contractual relations” that, under mass contracting methods, form “complex long-term legal relations” marked by the “position of ‘captivity’ or ‘dependence’ of clients, consumers” <2>Marques</2><3>(Marques, 2016, p. 77)</3>.

Updating this diagnosis for the digital environment reinforces that dependence is not limited to the economic cost of switching. It may arise from the very technical and informational design of the service, which makes migration costly and, at times, unrealistic. In this sense, when examining vulnerability by captivity in the digital sphere, Marques and Mucelin observe that, in contracts of successive performance, the search for security and for a future performance reduces the consumer to the position of “captive”, and that this dependence is understood in the context of current relations<1><2>446</2></1> <3>Mucelin</3><4>(Marques; Mucelin, 2022, p. 24)</4>. When the bond is prolonged and utility is realized over time, the product-service distinction only remains useful if it can see enjoyment as continuous supply and, within it, locate duties and conduct that do not fit in a description centered on the initial instant.

This long-term structure also prevents treating the interval between contracting and result as a legally irrelevant void. Marques proposes visualizing the contract as a dynamic relationship that is born, lives and dies, constituting a true process that develops over time, in which legal effects are produced during performance, before it and after it <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 222-223)</2>. This processual reading allows maintaining, in a controllable way, that the supplier's relevant conduct is not reduced to the initial “yes”, but is projected onto execution and onto the continuous administration of the conditions of enjoyment.

The legal usefulness of the product-service dichotomy is lost when it is treated as a dispute over labels capable of exhausting, by itself, the description of supply. In the regime of the IOC, this reduction is particularly costly because it shifts the focus away from what matters: preserving the acquired object as an enjoyment bundle and identifying the conduct that, in continued execution, maintains, degrades or reconfigures platform-governed utility. When enjoyment is read <1>p. 438</1> only as service in a generic sense, what was acquired tends to disappear from the language, and with it disappear relevant losses that do not manifest themselves as total interruption, but as significant degradation of the core of utility. At the opposite extreme, when supply is compressed into the paradigm of one-off delivery, the characteristic dimension of governed consumption, that is, the permanent administration of the conditions of access and use, ceases to be captured as part of performance itself. What is required is to prevent the dichotomy from producing methodological blindness and replacing the reconstruction of supply with a classification that blocks analysis, weakens the attribution of losses and compromises restoration compatible with continued enjoyment.

The first step in putting the dichotomy back in a functional key is to recognize that the CDC does not tie “product” to materiality, precisely to prevent economically relevant offers from escaping protection through formalism.

Once the breadth of “product” is recognized, the distinction from “service” remains relevant as a technical tool of attribution, provided it is not converted into a rigid ontology. Nunes observes that, in certain situations, even if it is possible to detach the service from the product, the distinction must be preserved because differences in the liability regime derive from it. At the same time, the author admits hybrid zones, in which the product is part of the service and may even be confused with it <1>Nunes</1><2>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 102])</2>. In a convergent key, Marques indicates that central expressions of the CDC require different readings depending on whether it is a contract for the provision of services or for the supply of products and that the very concept of quality defect assumes different meanings depending on the nature of the performance. The author also stresses that, although the discipline of formation and of control of contractual balance is the same in both modalities, the code does not ignore that the execution of these contracts is differentiated and characteristic <3>Miragem</3><4>(Marques; Benjamin; Miragem, 2013, p. 472)</4>. The result, here, is methodological. The dichotomy does not govern the regime of the IOC as a totalizing label; it calibrates specific effects, preserves the intelligibility of the acquired immaterial product and makes it possible to identify, in continued execution, relevant duties and conduct, without dissolving the object nor reducing supply to the initial instant.

Continued enjoyment, however, shifts the center of gravity of supply. In forms of consumption in which utility is realized over time and depends on permanent administration of the environment, protection is not played out only in the initial act nor exhausted at the instant in which utility becomes accessible for the first time. The product-service dichotomy can produce relevant effects, but these effects are concentrated where time matters: in the structure of duties and expectations that are stabilized during execution and in the way the system <1>p. 439</1> responds to partial degradations, gradual reconfigurations and localized interruptions of enjoyment. The usefulness of the distinction, in this context, lies not in declaring which label “wins”, but in preventing the reading of the offer and of the duties of adequacy from being flattened as if supply were an event.

The coexistence between the acquired object and continued execution appears clearly when the “product” sold is presented as a <1>premium</1> item, but its utility depends on routines of updating, compatibility and performance that only exist while the service remains technically operational. This is what happens with <2>skins</2>, especially those structured as evolving models that change form during the match itself. The consumer does not buy merely an “image” coupled to the character. They acquire a position of enjoyment that is only realized if the game environment remains capable of rendering models, effects, animations and interfaces that are reconfigured with each cycle of patches and system adjustments <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2022e)</4><5><6>447</6></5>.

The dogmatically relevant point is not to turn this item into a “service” by classificatory will, nor to pretend that the purchase is exhausted in the delivery of a static package. What matters is to perceive that, in objects of this type, utility is a bundle that depends on continuous execution of software. The form, the visual reading, the logic of transformation and the aesthetic experience happen as repeated performance in each match. Therefore, gradual alterations of the graphics engine, of the game's memory budget, of loading routines and of technical balance itself may, out of necessity of performance and compatibility, modify the way the item presents itself, limit behaviors, adjust features and, in extreme cases, require replacements and recompositions to preserve the integrity of the service <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2022k)</2><3><4>448</4></3>.

<1>p. 440</1> This type of example puts the product-service dichotomy back in the role the argument had already been demanding. The <2>skin</2> remains identifiable as an acquired object, not least because it is priced and communicated as a premium and distinctive item. At the same time, it does not exist as an enjoyable utility without the service of updating and maintaining the environment, which administers compatibility, fixes and adjustments. Riot's contractual framework itself assumes this structure by treating “virtual products” as elements that may evolve with fixes, graphical improvements and game rebalancing, and by declaring that updates and modifications may alter the service and restrict content and functionalities over time <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2024e)</4><5><6>449</6></5>.

In terms of attribution, this means that relevant losses may occur without total interruption. Frustration may manifest itself as localized degradation of the aesthetic experience, loss of consistency of the evolving model, alteration of features that were part of the practical promise of enjoyment, or reconfiguration that preserves the name of the item, but does not preserve the core of the utility that justified the purchase decision. In these cases, the product-service dichotomy helps precisely because it prevents two symmetrical blindnesses. The first blindness is to reduce everything to “delivered product” and treat subsequent technical modulations as an irrelevant exteriority. The second blindness is to dissolve the acquired object into “generic service” and, with that, make unsayable what, concretely, was lost, even if the bond continues formally in execution. The insertion of this empirical laboratory serves to show, with a case understandable even to those who do not live in the ecosystem, that the acquired and the executed coexist, and that protection needs to see this coexistence so that the protection of trust and the reading of adequacy are not flattened.

When the relationship is continued, the calibration of effects requires attention to elements that do not appear with the same clarity in one-off exchanges. Time projects duties of continuity and loyalty in execution, reorganizes the perception of adequacy, shifts the focus from “delivery” to “maintenance of utility”, and connects the protection of trust less to an isolated initial declaration and more to the consistency of performance throughout the bond. The product-service distinction can guide the reading of liability and warranty regimes without reducing the problem to materiality, and can help locate the core of non-performance when <1>p. 441</1> enjoyment is frustrated not by total absence of performance, but by relevant loss of quality, accessibility, functionalities or conditions of use. Calling everything a product as if it were instantaneous delivery may blind the analysis to the processual character of supply; calling everything a service in a generic sense may dissolve the acquired object and hinder the identification of what was lost.

The dichotomy, therefore, only retains usefulness if it is treated as a tool subordinate to the reconstruction of supply over time. It contributes to mapping effects and consequences, but does not by itself define the structure of the regime when utility materializes as sustained and governed enjoyment. This shift requires methodological justification: the refusal of the totalizing label is not conceptual relaxation, but a requirement when the regulated reality demands functional distinctions that general-abstract vocabulary tends to erase.

Once this shift is legitimized, the product-service tension comes to be read as a symptom of change in the mode of realization of supply. In platform-governed consumption, utility is not exhausted in making content accessible for the first time; it depends on the permanence of a technical-organizational environment that sustains, organizes and conditions enjoyment over time. The object remains intelligible as an immaterial product, an acquired enjoyment bundle, while performance manifests itself processually through continuous acts of maintenance, updating, curation, reconfiguration and execution of rules that modulate the experience of use.

Supply ceases to be described only by the inaugural instant and comes to be recognized as a durable practice of administering conditions of enjoyment, in which “quality” and “adequacy” become temporal attributes, subject to gradual degradations, cumulative restrictions and persistent alterations that do not take the form of total interruption. The dichotomy only retains usefulness if it follows this movement and allows identifying, without reductionism, the coexistence between an acquirable object and a continued execution that keeps it alive as a legally relevant utility.

This recognition finds explicit dogmatic support in the discipline of long-term contracts. Claudia Lima Marques states that “the obligational relationship is a continuous whole”, in which, “from its birth (and even before)”, the parties are bound “by a series of ancillary duties of conduct (<1>Nebenpflichten</1>), imposed by the general principle of good faith in the performance of obligations” <2>Marques</2><3>(Marques, 2016, p. 110)</3>. Protection cannot treat time as an empty interval, because it is precisely in execution that duties of cooperation, loyalty and protection of trust are stabilized, able to capture conduct that, in regimes of continued enjoyment, manifests itself as permanent administration of the conditions of access and use.

<1>p. 442</1> The reconfiguration deepens because long-term contracts carry structurally distinct expectations. Marques records that the contract is long-term, of successive and protracted execution, and therefore brings expectations different from those present in contracts of immediate execution, based more on trust, on repeated interaction and on the maintenance of the economic potential and the quality of services <2>Marques</2><3>(Marques, 2016, p. 106)</3>. In this framework, the contract is organized as a process, and platform-governed enjoyment can be described as a supply regime whose relevant conduct manifests itself in continued execution. The result is not to dilute the object, but to make explicit that the acquired utility presupposes permanent acts that are part of performance itself and that the product-service dichotomy only produces useful effects when it follows this processual character, without reducing protection to the inaugural instant.

With these premises, the product-service dichotomy can be stabilized as a rule of reading, and not as a classificatory dispute. Product fixes the intelligibility of what is acquired in the IOC, preserving the object as an economically valued and legally consumable enjoyment bundle, even if immaterial and dependent on technical mediations. Service, in turn, ceases to mean “there is no object” and comes to designate the mode of continued execution of supply, composed of practices of maintenance, organization and modulation of the conditions of enjoyment that are projected over time. The functional reading requires recognizing the coexistence of these dimensions without reciprocal reduction. This formula prevents two symmetrical distortions: it does not allow the supplier to escape protection by dissolving what was acquired into a generic performance and does not allow protection to be compressed into the paradigm of instantaneous delivery, incapable of capturing gradual degradations, persistent reconfigurations and relevant losses in the quality of enjoyment.

The understanding of supply as continued execution finds direct support when dogmatics shifts the focus from the isolated good to the activity of organizing, facilitating and sustaining access to an economically valued utility. In the Comentários ao Código de Defesa do Consumidor, Claudia Lima Marques makes explicit that the field of the CDC encompasses all legally consumable, useful and economically valued services and doings, even if they consist in simple use, simple organization, simple intermediation, simple information or ancillary conduct linked to a purpose valued in the market <1>Miragem</1><2>(Marques; Benjamin; Miragem, 2013, p. 186)</2>. In the same sense, in defining the verb to supply, she records that to supply means to provide, stock, furnish, give, administer, facilitate and afford, qualifying it as an activity independent of whoever holds ownership of the goods eventually used to provide the service and of its ancillary duties <3>Miragem</3><4>(Marques; Benjamin; Miragem, 2013, p. 179)</4>. When the core of the relationship lies in the administration of a structure <5>p. 443</5> that makes enjoyment possible, the legally relevant conduct is located in the very organization of access, and not in the material ownership of the means employed.

This reading is completed when it is shown that, in complex and lasting relationships, the supplier may be precisely the organizer of the chains that make consumption viable, even if the final performance is executed by third parties. Marques describes this structure by stating that these are services generally carried out with the use of third parties to achieve the true contractual objective, which leads to the organization of invisible chains of direct and indirect suppliers <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 76)</2>. In a convergent key, discussing network activities, Nunes maintains that, in reality, the service provided is the supply and that the assembly of the entire network exists to make the realization of that supply viable <3>Nunes</3><4>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 114])</4>. With this, it becomes consistent to read platform-based continued enjoyment as supply that is realized through infrastructure and the governance of access. The product-service dichotomy remains in the system as a tool for specific effects, without erasure of the object, and the immaterial product remains identifiable, merely complemented by the service dimension, understood as a continuous activity of organizing and administering the conditions of enjoyment.

Repositioning the dichotomy as an instrument of reading requires, finally, justifying why dogmatics needs to operate with controllable cuts in contexts of complexity and continued enjoyment. From the methodological perspective already established, the dogmatic operation is a technique aimed at decidability, which increases uncertainties in a way compatible with the binding to norms and with institutional pressure for decision. In platform-governed consumption, insisting on generic labels or rigid classifications tends to paralyze protection, because the vocabulary needs to cut the phenomenon so as to preserve what is relevant for attribution and restoration. The conceptual engineering of the IOC, in this framework, is not a luxury, but a condition of possibility of non-arbitrary protection in environments of opacity and mutability.

In regimes of continued enjoyment, the counterfactual stabilization of normative expectations, already established as a methodological lock of the regime of the IOC, makes it possible to treat as legally relevant duties of continuity, adequacy and loyalty even when the technical environment admits constant reconfigurations. The conflict ceases to be only the event and comes to be the resistance of normative expectations to the frustration produced by the very mode of functioning of supply.

Finally, in scenarios of opacity and insecurity, legal decision cannot be presented as the elimination of conflict, but as its conversion into operable alternatives, <1>p. 444</1> since decisions absorb insecurity not because they eliminate the conflict, but because they transform it <2>Jr.</2><3>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 306])</3>. Therefore, the product-service dichotomy, when treated as a totalizing label, tends to produce blindness or impossibility of decision. When treated as a calibrating instrument, on the contrary, it helps make it possible to decide what, under rigid classifications or undifferentiated terms, would remain undecidable.

With this, the dichotomy is preserved in the system without coming to govern the system. It remains useful for calibrating effects and locating specific regimes, but ceases to function as a totalizing answer for a supply whose utility is realized over time and under infrastructural governance. The immaterial product preserves the intelligibility of what was acquired as an economically valued enjoyment bundle. Service describes the continuous activity of organizing, facilitating and administering the conditions of access and use, where ancillary duties, expectations of continuity and conduct relevant to adequacy and quality are installed. The consequence is a rule of reading that makes the phenomenon decidable without flattening it. Initial delivery does not exhaust performance, and continued execution does not erase the object.

With the dichotomy repositioned in this instrumental role, the next step ceases to be classificatory and becomes one of attribution. It is necessary to identify when the very architecture of supply, in its permanent administration, manifests exploitative purposes and patterns of modulation that exceed the normal risk of the bond and are converted into a controllable legal criterion. It is this transition that requires advancing to the category of abusive teleology, capable of bringing platform governance back to the plane of legally relevant conduct and of preparing, next, the delimitation of relevant losses and the <1>standards</1> of control and restoration compatible with continued enjoyment.

The article-by-article dogmatic reading developed by Claudia Lima Marques, Antonio Herman V. Benjamin and Bruno Miragem, in <1>Comentários ao Código de Defesa do Consumidor</1> (2013), combines doctrine and case law under the key of the dialogue of sources, providing technical support to deal with complex supply scenarios without allowing the product-service dichotomy to become a classificatory obstacle. In parallel, the reflection of Claudia Lima Marques and Bruno Miragem, in <2>O novo direito privado e a proteção dos vulneráveis</2> (2012), reinforces that structural vulnerabilities may be part of the very arrangement of the relationship, functioning as a criterion of dogmatic orientation for the effective containment of asymmetries, especially when the bond is durable and mediated by technical architectures. <3>↩</3>

The notion of “captivity” employed by Marques and Mucelin does not designate mere contractual discomfort, but a situation of dependence structured around the maintenance of or access to services (including those offered by platforms) that, in the contemporary context, are perceived as conditions of full enjoyment and self-realization. In this picture, in contracts of successive performance, the search for security and for future performances tends to convert the consumer into a “captive client”, and this dependence is only adequately understood on the basis of the concrete arrangement of socially produced expectations: “[I]n these contracts of successive performance the relationship is driven by the search for security, by the search for a future performance, status or a certain quality in services, which reduces the consumer to a position of ‘captive’ - client of the supplier and of its group of collaborators or economic agents. The position of dependence of ‘captivity’ can only be understood in the examination of the context of current relations, in which certain services provided in the market ensure (or promise) to the consumer and their family ‘status’, ‘security’, ‘renewed credit’, ‘a certain and qualified school or university education’, ‘assured housing’, ‘leisure’ or even ‘health’ or ‘information’ in the future.” (Marques; Mucelin, p. 97-98). <1>↩</1>

In the official support material, Riot describes the <1>Ultimate</1> <2>Skin</2> as something that adds an unprecedented layer of content to the game, which reinforces that it is not a mere static texture, but a set of behaviors and presentations that need to be executed by the environment in each match. The specific FAQ for the popular <3>Elementalist Lux</3> states that <4>Ultimate skins</4> “add something completely brand new to the game” <5>Riot Games</5><6>(Riot Games, 2022e)</6>. The description is relevant because, in detailing how the <7>skin</7> works, the official support makes clear that enjoyment depends on internal game processes, such as energy accumulation and selection of transformations during the match, that is, it depends on interface and <8>scripts</8> that run within the game, in a continuous service perspective. The mechanic is not a “contemplative file”, but a performance guided by rules and by active rendering, so that the maintenance of utility is inseparable from the maintenance of the technical environment. <9>↩</9>

In an official text about the update of an <1>Ultimate Skin</1>, developers describe that skins of this level can be treated almost as a new champion in terms of work and technical load, and that there is a material performance ceiling that conditions choices. In the post, it is stated that <2>Ultimate skins</2> are basically new champions, maintaining that, beneath the interface, there is a memory limit per champion (“memory budget”) <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2022k)</4>. This is evidence that the preservation of the premium “product” depends on engineering and compatibility decisions, which may impose reconfigurations to ensure the overall performance of the service. This reinforces the integrated reading of supply, since it makes visible that the acquired object, even if stable, is technically dependent on continued maintenance and, therefore, vulnerable to modulations justified by systemic requirements. <5>↩</5>

It should be recalled that, beyond the general reservation of updating and modulating the service, the Terms assume, in the Virtual Content regime, specific powers to reorganize the game's content, by stating that the company “we have the right to delete, alter, move, remove, re-package, re-price or transfer any and all Game Content, including Virtual Content”, and by declaring, directly, that “your Virtual Products may (and probably will) evolve over time”, including for “game balance, bug fixes [and] graphical improvements” as typical reasons <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. <3>↩</3>

<1>Governed enjoyment bundle</1>
<1>Immaterial Object of Consumption (IOC)</1>

The description of platform-governed continuous consumption has already established that the acquisition is not exhausted in an event of delivery, since it inaugurates a position of sustained enjoyment in an environment that implements rules, orders priorities and executes sanctions permanently. It has also already been demonstrated, with semiotic vulnerability, that the decisive asymmetry in these regimes is not reduced to episodic informational deficits, but arises from a structural inequality of intelligibility and agency in the face of signs, metrics and regimes of visibility administered by the ecosystem itself. From these premises, the construction of a conceptual house is required, capable of converting such a regime into operable legal language, able to represent the form of existence of the object, delimit relevant losses and prepare criteria of attribution and restoration compatible with sustained enjoyment.

The adequate legal qualification of the immaterial object of consumption requires more than a sociotechnical description of the environment of enjoyment. What is sought is a category capable of organizing, from the regime actually experienced, the reading of what was offered, of what becomes legally relevant as loss and of what should guide restoration when enjoyment is degraded by unilateral reconfiguration, curation, <1>enforcement</1> or design. By treating the object as a position of sustained enjoyment in a technical-organizational arrangement that administers access, permanence, visibility and circulation, it becomes possible to bring the analysis back to controllable elements of supply, preventing protection from depending exclusively on explicit contractual commands or on episodic assessments of information provided.

<1>p. 408</1> The player's account in the Riot ecosystem offers a methodologically privileged example of an immaterial object of consumption in its most “infrastructural” form. It is not reduced to a login credential. It is the organizational point that holds the enjoyment bundle together, because it concentrates, in a single institutional record, the inventory of licensed virtual content, the progression markers, the social identifiers and the reputation signals by which the user's presence is read, displayed and recognized in the environment. In practical terms, most of what is understood as “acquisition” in this type of consumption does not subsist as a detachable object outside this operative account and the maintained service.

This is not described only by the user's experience. The contractual discipline of the service itself gives form to this arrangement by establishing that access to the Services, including so-called Virtual Content, occurs by limited and revocable license, conditioned on compliance with the Terms, and that termination of the account entails automatic cancellation of the license and loss of access to the associated content <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2><3><4>420</4></3>. The account, in this way, functions as the minimal legal infrastructure of the enjoyment bundle, since it organizes the practical entitlement to access, but does not consolidate a regime of possession by the consumer over the content, which remains dependent on the execution environment and on the supplier's rules of private governance.

The contractual definition of Virtual Content reinforces this reading. Champions, <1>skins</1>, emotes and in-game currency make up the catalog of goods that only become enjoyable as an access license associated with the account, and not as things transportable outside it <2>Riot Games</2><3>(Riot Games, 2024e)</3><4><5>421</5></4>. The enjoyment bundle appears, then, as a collection of positions accessible through an <6>p. 409</6> institutional identifier and an infrastructure that stabilizes what is visible, usable and recognizable in the ecosystem. The account is the unit that aggregates these elements. Therefore, it can be described as the central IOC and, at the same time, as an “infrastructure-concept” in miniature. What one “has” is inseparable from the regime that makes enjoyment operative.

When passing from the declared norm to the norm in operation, the infrastructural nature of this position becomes even more intelligible. Riot maintains an official service status page, with current messages and a history of incidents, allowing public verification of the integrity of the systems on which enjoyment depends <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, [202-?]f)</2><3><4>422</4></3>. The use value of the bundle, in this condition, is not stock, it is flow. It requires continuity of servers, institutional connectivity and maintenance of the environment. When the service presents unavailability, it is not only access that fails, but the virtual content itself loses immediate utility, because the environment that makes it enjoyable ceases to operate.

The account is also treated as an object of security and institutional recovery. In official guidance, Riot recognizes the hypothesis of a compromised account and states that, in this case, the user must open a ticket to recover it, which reveals that the player's “existence” in the ecosystem is a record susceptible to incidents and dependent on institutional restoration procedures, in addition to good protection practices <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2025n)</2><3><4>423</4></3>. It is not, therefore, a good under the consumer's exclusive custody, but a position managed by rules of integrity, validation and intervention, which the supplier admits as a regular part of the functioning of the service.

The community repository describes the “summoner” as the persistent element, reporting that “summoner accounts” are used to store activities in data and scoreboards, and indicating that, at the end of matches, this profile gains experience, which makes up its progression in the ecosystem (League of Legends Wiki, [202-?]c; League of Legends Wiki, <1>p. 410</1> [202-?]b)<2><3>424</3></2>. This technical vocabulary helps name and make observable what, in the consumer's experience, appears as an accumulation of history, reputation and value. The account aggregates and stabilizes cumulative variables of enjoyment and visibility, which depend on a continuous technical-organizational regime to remain intelligible and operative.

This set makes it possible to understand why the player's account is, here, the maximum example of the IOC. It is the support that makes the bundle enjoyable, commensurable and sanctionable, because it organizes the unit through which the environment grants access, records progression, consolidates inventory and recognizes belonging. When there is blocking, termination or significant degradation of the regime, it is in this unit that the relevant loss tends to manifest itself. The account is not a peripheral detail of performance. It is the very infrastructure of consumption.

The formulation of this category presupposes conceptual sobriety. The focus falls on verifiable structures of governance of the environment and on relevant effects on the consumer's position of enjoyment, so that the category operates as an instrument of qualification, attribution and restoration in continuous consumption. To fulfill this function, the concept must distinguish ordinary variations of the digital regime from significant degradations of the enjoyment bundle that give economic and social meaning to the object.

The construction of this key of qualification remains situated within the discipline of consumption, without intending to inaugurate an autonomous microsystem for the digital. The anchoring point is the concept of product, as provided for in Article 3, paragraph 1, of the Consumer Protection Code, because it is within this framework that it becomes possible to recognize an object of enjoyment that is not reduced to a material medium, but also does not dissolve into an undifferentiated language of “service” capable of erasing what was actually acquired. By starting from the immaterial product as a reference, the intelligibility of supply is preserved and space is opened to describe the object according to its function and according to the relationship it establishes, keeping controllable the identification of the promised enjoyment bundle, the characterization of relevant degradations and the orientation of proportional responses when enjoyment is altered by reconfigurations, curations or sanctions executed by design.

The legal usefulness of this category is not exhausted in naming a contemporary phenomenon of consumption. It must operate in a dual function: to qualify the object in a way <1>p. 411</1> compatible with its form of existence and, at the same time, to provide an interpretive key capable of reorganizing the reading of the offer, of relevant losses and of the possibilities of restoration. From this perspective, the Immaterial Object of Consumption does not function as a descriptive label external to the regime, but as an infrastructure-concept that makes it possible to recognize how promise, execution and governance are articulated to produce or degrade the enjoyment bundle, even if formal access to the “content” remains available.

In its Terms of Use, Riot qualifies the use of the services as a “limited [...] revocable license” and links its continuity to the state of the account, by providing that, if the account is terminated, the license is automatically canceled <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. In simple language, this means that access to the ecosystem is structured as a conditioned permission of use, and not as ownership of an autonomous good. The account functions as the institutional mechanism that concentrates this permission and, consequently, the enjoyment bundle. <3>↩</3>

The Terms define “Virtual Content” as typical digital goods of the game, including “champions, skins, emotes” and “in-game currency”, and state that this is offered as an access license “associated with your account” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. In League of Legends, “Champions” are the playable characters; “skins” are cosmetic variations of these characters; “emotes” are customizable symbols used for visual communication within the game; and “in-game currency” is the balance used to acquire content within the ecosystem. The relevant legal point is that all these items, even when perceived as acquisitions, are described as accesses that remain tied to the account record. This reinforces the account as the infrastructure of the enjoyment bundle, because it functions as the “institutional container” in which the inventory exists and is recognized. This contractual framing produces a relevant semiotic friction. Although the normative text qualifies these items as a revocable license linked to the account, the ordinary experience of acquisition in the client and in the store is organized by the language and rituals of purchase and sale, with commands such as “buy”, “acquire” and “unlock”, which trigger in the consumer expectations typical of stable patrimonial acquisition. With this, the platform mobilizes, at the moment of decision, the social grammar of purchase to induce a perception of possession and permanence, but preserves, in the legal structure of the bond, the possibility of unilateral recomposition and of loss through termination of the account. In this tension, the sign “buy” is not a mere communicational detail. It functions as a category marker that tends to frame virtual content as an acquired good, when, in the regime described by the contract, it is conditioned and institutionally controlled access, which increases the risk of frustrated legitimate expectation and of informational asymmetry in the formation of consent. <3>↩</3>

The official service status page contains sections such as “Current messages” and records “No recent issues or incidents” when the service is stable <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, [202-?]f)</2>. This matters because it makes public a structural fact of continuous consumption, namely that the utility of the enjoyment bundle depends on the technical availability of the environment. When the service is unavailable, it is not only that “the user cannot log in”, but that the virtual content itself ceases to be enjoyable, since it only operates within the service. The page functions as an institutional indicator that the continuity of the object depends on an infrastructure continuously maintained by the supplier. <3>↩</3>

In official guidance, Riot states that, if the account has been compromised, the user must “submit a ticket [...] to recover it” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2025n)</2>, which means that the account is treated as a record of identity and access that can be breached, corrected and restored by the supplier's internal procedures. The relevant difference between the Riot account and a common digital registration is that, in this context, the registration concentrates the enjoyment bundle, and the company itself assumes institutional routines to protect and reestablish this position, which reinforces that the account is not “just a password”, but the infrastructure of the consumer's existence in the ecosystem. <3>↩</3>

The account is responsible for concentrating the bond of progression and unlocks in the environment, understood on the basis of the completion of tasks and the accumulation of “experience”, a progression marker accumulated at the end of matches, which serves to organize the development of the profile <1>League of Legends Wiki</1><2>(League of Legends Wiki, [202-?]c)</2>. These are concrete variables through which the environment stabilizes accumulated value and identity. This helps make intelligible why the account is the central IOC of the ecosystem, since it is the record that aggregates inventory, history and progression, which is why it is also the point at which enjoyment exists as a position. <3>↩</3>

<1>Unlawful act of architecture</1>

Platform governance has already been described as a form of private regulation that combines terms, technical architecture and continuous execution of rules, producing an environment in which the acquired utility is realized under permanent modulation. In continuity with the recognition that, in IOCs, architecture and governance are not “exteriorities” of the object, but a material dimension of supply itself, the next step consists in bringing this description back to the plane of legally relevant conduct, distinguishing institutional diagnosis from applicable dogmatic criterion.

The <1>Lex Plataformae</1> operates as a descriptive category to identify the mode of exercise of power and of production of normativity in the ecosystem, that is, the scenario in which the legal <2>p. 445</2> phenomenon manifests itself. Abusive teleology, in turn, must operate as a controllable category of attribution. Its role is to qualify exploitative purposes materialized in the very architecture of supply, without being confused with moral judgment about technology and without becoming an expansive label indifferent to limits. With this, legal control can fall on the purpose and structural arrangement of supply, without being limited to isolated conduct and without anticipating, at this point, the exhaustive fit into quality defects, safety defects, abusive practices and abusive clauses.
